article.overview: A surface topography mapper is a payload whose main output is a map of ground height and relief, measured at the surface or from a platform close to it, such as a rover, a lander or a mast. Its job is to turn ranging measurements into a local three-dimensional description of the ground. Scope of this entry: surface-based topography sensing whose measurement principle is ranging to the ground, for example laser-dot or laser-line triangulation, structured light and close-range active 3D sensing, and the products of these sensors (local height maps, slope information and obstacle heights). Out of scope, with cross-references: orbital laser altimeters and their ranging products (see 047, Laser altimeter); lidar scanners as a class (see 046, Lidar scanner); terrain mapping cameras and stereo imagers that produce digital terrain models from orbit or from a lander (see 028, Terrain mapping camera, and 029, Stereo camera); photogrammetry systems (see 049, Photogrammetry system); digital terrain mapping systems (see 050, Digital terrain mapping system); imaging cameras whose topography is derived only in post-processing (see 026, Panoramic camera, and 027, High-resolution camera); close-range microscopic imaging of the surface (see 033, Microscopic imager). Status statement: the sources accessed for this article do not confirm a dedicated surface topography mapper that has flown on the Moon. The examples are a structured-light hazard-detection prototype tested in a lunar-analogue outdoor terrain, a JPL concept study with no published performance numbers, and a 2024 study of topography add-ons for compact rover laser spectrometers. These are development-stage references, not flight hardware.
article.description: Most surface topography sensors use triangulation. A light source, usually a laser, projects a known pattern onto the ground, and a camera views the pattern from a known offset. Because the offset, the projection angle and the optics are fixed and calibrated, the position of the pattern in the camera image encodes the distance to the ground at each point. A flat surface produces one expected pattern; a raised rock or a depression shifts the pattern in a measurable way. Structured-light systems project more than one stripe or dot at once, so that one image can give several height samples. Laser-line systems project a single line, and a full map is built by moving the sensor along the surface (general explanation; not attributed to a specific source). The lunar setting makes active illumination attractive: sunlit and shadowed areas can appear in the same image, and passive stereo struggles when the scene has little texture or is poorly lit. The structured-light prototype in physical_specifications.examples[0] was designed for this case, including dark regions such as shadowed craters [1]. The Example 1 paper states that structured-light sensors have been proposed for hazard detection in planetary missions and cites Mars Pathfinder as one example [1]; that citation was not independently verified for this article.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: A surface topography mapper supports three main groups of purposes. (1) Traverse safety and obstacle detection: a rover needs to know where rocks, pits and steep slopes lie ahead. The structured-light prototype was built to find obstacles about 10 cm high in the path of a rover moving at up to 20 cm/s [1]. (2) Close-range topography for geology: a 2024 study on compact laser spectrometers considers adding three-dimensional topography measurement techniques to rover-mounted spectroscopy [3]. The stated purpose is to enhance those instruments; the search summary does not describe how the topography would be used with the spectra, and its accuracy is not stated, so this remains an objective rather than a demonstrated capability. (3) Local ground truth for orbital products: close-range height data could in principle be compared with orbital DTMs. None of the sources accessed demonstrate this use, so it is noted as a possibility and not as a verified application.
article.operating_principle: The Example 1 prototype illustrates the general triangulation principle [1]. A laser projector with a diffraction grating produces 11 red (660 nm) dots, each at a fixed angle, aimed at the ground ahead of the rover. The camera is mounted with a horizontal baseline of 26 cm from the projector and a pitch of 28 degrees [1]. On flat ground each dot falls at a predicted place in the image. When a dot strikes an obstacle it lands closer to the camera and its image position shifts along a line parallel to the baseline (an epipolar line). The size of that shift, the pixel disparity, relates to the distance and height of the obstacle [1]. The paper uses an analytic threshold: for an obstacle of 10 cm height the analytic disparity is 15.9 pixels; the neutral spacing between adjacent dots is 20 pixels; the empirically validated detection threshold is 15 pixels, described by the authors as 75% of the ideal spacing [1]. To separate the dots from sunlight, the prototype requires the projected dots to be brighter than the surrounding scene in a single image. A binary threshold selects the bright pixels and a clustering step groups them and removes small clusters [1]. The method needs no second frame with the projector off, which would have required the rover to stop [1].
article.scientific_importance: Topography is central to planetary geology and to surface operations. Orbital altimetry and stereo mapping give broad coverage, while a surface mapper gives dense, close-range measurements at the scale of a rover's traverse. The gap between those scales is where a surface mapper is most useful. The evidence for this value is currently limited. The structured-light prototype has been tested in analogue terrain, and its published results concern obstacle detection rather than full height maps [1]. The scientific value of a topography mapper on the Moon therefore depends on future flight tests and on demonstrated mapping accuracy, neither of which is established in the sources accessed.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a surface topography mapper. The three examples use different principles and are at different development stages; they are not comparable as one product, so no combined table is presented. Each value is tied to the named example and its source. Where a source does not publish a value, the value is null and the text says 'not publicly specified'.

examples.name: Structured-light virtual bumper prototype (Nefian et al., NASA Ames and Stinger Ghaffarian Technologies)
examples.status: Engineering prototype, not flown. Built for hazard avoidance on planetary rovers; tested extensively in day and night conditions in lunar-analogue environments. Mounted on NASA's K-REX2 rover and tested at NASA Ames Research Center's Roverscape, a two-acre outdoor planetary analogue terrain [1].

published_configuration.projector: Commercially available red (660 nm) laser projector with an 11-dot diffraction grating [1]
published_configuration.camera: Commercial machine-vision camera (Allied Vision Manta) with Sony ICX267 image sensor [1]
published_configuration.optics: 3.5 mm focal length lens at F/5.6; ISO 400-equivalent gain for test images [1]
published_configuration.geometry: 26 cm horizontal baseline between camera and projector; pitch angle 28 degrees [1]
published_configuration.capture_rate_note: Images captured at 0.5 Hz, which the paper describes as reflecting a mission requirement [1]
published_configuration.obstacle_test_set: Four types: large angular rocks, ejecta blocks, smaller angular rocks and multi-rock aggregates; obstacle albedos below 10% to 33% [1]

reported_performance.note: Measured test results from the Roverscape tests, not flight results [1].
reported_performance.positive_obstacle_detection_accuracy_per: about 97; not significantly different between day and night [1]
reported_performance.false_alarm_rate_percent: 1.7 at night; 4.1 in the worst day test [1]
reported_performance.f1_score: 0.92 average for day images; 0.96 average for night images [1]
reported_performance.evaluation_data: 1158 day images across two tests; 1544 night images, of which 30 to 40 percent included obstacles [1]

examples.laser_optical_power: not publicly specified in the source text read; the paper names laser power and wavelength as design parameters and lists higher-power projectors as future work [1]

examples.reference_design_inputs: The pre-test analysis uses a lunar reflectance model and soil albedo data for Apollo sample sites shown in Figure 1 of the paper. These are design inputs, not properties of the prototype [1].

examples.name: Topography add-ons for compact rover laser spectrometers (Sensors, 2024)
examples.status: Published study in Sensors (volume 24, issue 9, article 2872), University of Stuttgart Institute of Applied Optics according to the search summary used here. The study considers adding three-dimensional topography measurement techniques to compact laser spectrometers integrated into space-exploration rovers [3].

examples.reported_performance: not publicly specified in the sources read. A search summary reported that fringe projection has been used on NASA's PIXL instrument on Mars to determine object distance to within 500 micrometres; this was not verified against PIXL primary documentation and is not used as a value [3]
examples.notes: Laser spectrometers that analyse rock composition are covered under the spectrometer entries in category 3. This example covers only the topography add-on.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No single dimension set applies to a surface topography mapper. The Example 1 prototype's published geometry is a 26 cm camera-to-projector baseline and a 28 degree pitch [1]; no enclosure dimensions are published in the source text read. The JPL SLIM concept has no published dimensions [2]. The 2024 rover spectrometer study publishes no dimensions in the sources read [3]. The geometry that matters for triangulation is the baseline, pitch and calibration, not the enclosure size.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: not publicly specified for any example. The Example 1 paper does not publish mass [1]. No mass is recorded for SLIM [2] or for the 2024 study [3].
physical_specifications.power_requirements: not publicly specified for any example. The Example 1 paper presents the system as requiring low onboard power and computation, and identifies projector power as a key design parameter, but gives no power value in the source text read [1].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A surface topography mapper must work in vacuum, with large temperature changes and without the diffuse skylight that an atmosphere provides. The prototype's test conditions illustrate the main operational issues [1]. Mixed illumination: sunlit ground and shadowed craters can appear in the same image; the prototype addresses this with a single-image method that depends on projected dots being brighter than the scene, so projector power is a key requirement [1]. Dust and albedo: lunar regolith is fine and powdered; the outdoor tests used a layer of pea gravel over an area with average albedo of 8%, which the authors say is similar to lunar regolith but is not a regolith simulant [1]. The authors identify the gravel as a source of false alarms, because granules create speckle and act as occluders [1]. Motion and exposure: long exposure causes motion blur, which smears dots along the epipolar line and can cause errors; fast shutter speeds are identified as important [1]. Frame and drive rate: images were captured at 0.5 Hz and the prototype was tested at speeds up to 20 cm/s [1]; a flight system would have to meet the real-time requirements that the paper names as a central constraint [1]. Daylight visibility: projected dots were harder to see in daylight, even with a monochromatic laser and a narrow-band filter, and daytime false-alarm rates were higher [1]. Power and computation: the paper presents the system as requiring low onboard power and computation; no budget is given in the source text read [1].
article.limitations: Analogue testing only: the published results come from an outdoor analogue facility, not from the Moon. The test surface used gravel rather than regolith, and the illumination was approximated rather than reproduced [1]. Obstacle detection, not mapping: the prototype reports obstacle presence and size in the rover path; it does not describe a full height map, its vertical accuracy or its coverage per frame [1]. Limited power margin: the paper names higher-power laser projectors as future work to handle high-reflectance surfaces and multiple reflections [1]. Daytime performance: daytime false alarms were higher than at night and dot visibility fell in bright light [1]. No flight heritage: no surface topography mapper in the sources accessed has been flown on the Moon.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A surface topography mapper of the kinds described here would be a rover-mounted or lander-mounted sensor. No orbiter configuration is assumed. Rover integration: the prototype was mounted on the leading edge of the K-REX2 rover, with the projector and camera facing forward to view the ground ahead [1]. For a flight system, the important interfaces would be mounting geometry, calibrated baseline and pitch angle, power, data handling and optical protection from dust. The prototype is a calibrated system, so a change of mounting geometry would require recalibration; this is an inference from the calibration requirement described in the paper [1]. The sources accessed do not give any flight mounting interface, mass allocation or power budget.
transportation_process: Integrate the sensor onto a rover or lander structure on Earth, with the projector and camera fixed at a calibrated baseline and pitch.
Launch with the carrying vehicle; stowage and protection requirements follow that vehicle's specification (not established for any example in this entry).
Transfer to the Moon and land with the carrying vehicle.
Deploy or verify the sensor's view of the ground, check calibration, and connect power, timing and data handling.
Operate in traverse or survey modes, with optical protection from dust and thermal control as required.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Stowage, release and deployment mechanisms are not described for any example in this entry. The Example 1 prototype was a rover-mounted test configuration on K-REX2 in analogue terrain, not a deployed flight configuration [1].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The K-REX2 rover at NASA Ames Roverscape is the test platform for the Example 1 prototype [1]. The JPL SLIM concept is a research-task illustration on a Mars rover [2]. No lunar flight deployment of a dedicated surface topography mapper is established in the sources accessed.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lunar rover, lander or spacecraft is asserted. Any such claim would need verified interface documents for the named vehicle.

article.historical_significance: The structured-light hazard detection work (physical_specifications.examples[0]) is the most complete published test in the sources accessed for a surface-based active topography sensor aimed at lunar-like terrain [1]. Its significance lies in showing, in analogue tests, that a camera and laser dot projector can detect obstacles in both bright and dark conditions, with reported accuracy values [1]. The JPL SLIM concept is an early research task illustrating structured-light rover navigation [2]. The 2024 rover spectrometer study shows continuing interest in adding topography to rover spectrometers [3]. A news summary also reports NASA's KNaCK lidar mapping prototype, which is covered under 046 (Lidar scanner) and is not described in detail here [4].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Flight status: no surface topography mapper was confirmed as flown on the Moon in the sources accessed. Prototype mass, power and resolution: the Example 1 paper does not publish mass, dimensions, power, laser optical power or detector resolution in the text read; these are null. Operating range: the working range in metres is not stated in the text read; the paper gives geometry and the 10 cm obstacle analysis, not a complete range specification. Topography accuracy: the Example 1 paper reports obstacle-detection performance, not vertical accuracy of a height map. Example 1 (SLIM): no published numbers, hardware description or test status on the page accessed [2]. Example 2 (2024 study): the abstract was not read; claims are limited to topic and objective [3]. Unverified secondary claims: the PIXL 500 micrometre fringe-projection figure, the KNaCK centimetre-level precision claim and the Mars Pathfinder structured-light reference were not verified against primary documents and are not used as values [1][4]. Publication details: the venue and publication year of the Example 1 paper were not confirmed from the text read; the NASA record identifier is 20170009200 [1]. Cross-references: lidar scanners are in 046, laser altimeters in 047, photogrammetry in 049, digital terrain mapping systems in 050 and terrain mapping cameras in 028; this entry does not duplicate them.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: No flown, surface-deployed dedicated surface topography mapper was confirmed in the sources accessed. All examples are engineering prototypes, research tasks or published studies, and are labelled as such.

Example 1 (structured-light virtual bumper, Nefian et al.): the paper's mass, dimensions, power, laser optical power, detector resolution in pixels and operating range in metres are not stated in the text read; these are recorded as null or 'not publicly specified'.

Example 1: the paper reports obstacle-detection accuracy, false-alarm rates and F1 scores from analogue tests (Roverscape at NASA Ames, pea gravel surface, 8% albedo). It does not report height-map vertical accuracy.
Example 1: the venue and publication year of the paper were not confirmed from the PDF text read; the NASA record identifier is 20170009200.
Example 2 (JPL SLIM): the gallery page gives no hardware description, numbers or test status. The image is an artist's concept of a Mars rover and is not evidence of a lunar configuration.

Example 3 (2024 Sensors study): the publisher page returned HTTP 403 to the automated fetch, so the abstract, authors and methods were not read. The topic is taken from a search summary, and the institution attribution is per that summary.

The PIXL fringe-projection figure (distance to within 500 micrometres), the KNaCK centimetre-level precision claim and the Mars Pathfinder structured-light reference are secondary claims that were not verified against primary documents and are not used as values.
Image rights: the SLIM image credit is not stated on the source page and reuse conditions were not verified. It is not treated as public domain.
Transportation: no flight mounting interface, mass allocation, power budget or lander compatibility was verified for any example. No compatibility claim is made.
